parts.title: Which microbes turn DMSO into DMS and then into methane in saltmarsh mud?
parts.abstract:
Saltmarshes are coastal wetlands where plants grow very fast, and they hold large amounts of sulfur-containing compounds made by living things. One of these, called DMSP, is made in large quantities by algae, plants and bacteria. DMSP may be a starting material for two other compounds: DMSO and DMS. When microbes breathe without oxygen, they can use DMSO in place of oxygen. This turns DMSO into DMS. The DMS can then escape into the air, or it can be broken down by microbes that feed on small sulfur compounds. The main products of these reactions are gases present only in tiny amounts. Carbon dioxide (CO2) and methane (CH4) trap heat and warm the planet, while DMS reflects sunlight and cools it, so these gases have opposite effects on the global climate.

In this study, we looked at how sulfur compounds made by living things are broken down and recycled in saltmarsh mud. We also followed DMSO being turned into DMS in sealed bottles of mud kept without oxygen. The mud held up to about 300 times more DMSO than earlier measurements in seawater had found. In our bottles, DMSO was first turned into DMS, and the DMS was then used up while methane was made at the same time.

We tracked which microbes were present and how many copies of the genes for DMSO-breaking enzymes they carried. These results showed that microbes with the Dms-type of DMSO-breaking enzyme were the most common (for example, the groups Desulfobulbales and Enterobacterales). When we blocked the microbes that normally breathe sulfate, using a chemical called molybdate, microbes with the Tor-type of DMSO-breaking enzyme (for example, Rhodobacterales) became more common instead. A third group, Vibrionales, became more common in both treatments. We also pieced together genomes of individual microbes from the mixed DNA of the whole community. The ones belonging to Vibrio carried all the genes for the parts of DMSO-breaking enzymes.

We added less than 1.3 molecules of methane for every molecule of DMSO we added. At the same time, the methane-making microbes that feed on small sulfur compounds, called Methanosarcinales, became the most common. In the DNA of our bottles, genes called mtsDH became more common. These genes carry the instructions for enzymes that move a small carbon-and-sulfur piece (a methyl group) from DMS. This points to their role in making methane from DMS. The genomes we pieced together from the group Methanolobus carried the full set of genes for the enzymes needed to make methane from small sulfur compounds.
parts.introduction_first: Saltmarshes are coastal wetlands where plants grow very fast. They help protect the coast, they recycle nutrients and other substances between living things, water and soil, and they provide food for people [1, 2]. Saltmarshes are often divided into zones. Each zone is flooded by the tides a different number of times and has its own plants, and this shapes which nutrients and microbes live there [3–6]. Most of the plant and animal material that grows in a saltmarsh is broken down in the mud [7]. In the mud of the sea, most of this breakdown (about 50%) is driven by microbes that breathe sulfate, a sulfur compound, in place of oxygen [8]. Other substances that microbes can use for breathing, such as DMSO, give them more energy, so they may also play a key role [9, 10].
parts.conclusion:
Conclusions

Saltmarshes hold a lot of DMSO, which shows that DMSO matters for microbes that breathe without oxygen and for the DMS they make along the way. We found that many microbes in the environment carry the genes to break down DMSO, and the Dms-type of DMSO-breaking enzyme was especially common. When DMS levels were high, the share of methane-making microbes that carry the mtsDH genes (a group called Methanosarcinacaea) went up. This shows that DMS can serve as food for these microbes without competing with other microbes for it.

However, in nature, microbes may make less methane from DMS, and future studies need to measure how much. DMS escaping into the air is thought to cool the climate. If microbes turn DMS into the greenhouse gases methane (CH4) and carbon dioxide (CO2), that cooling effect would be cancelled out.
parts.introduction_rest:
When microbes breathe without oxygen, they can use DMSO in place of oxygen, and this turns DMSO into DMS [11]. DMS is a gas present only in tiny amounts. It is a starting material for secondary organic aerosols, which are tiny particles that form in the air from gases. These particles may help cool the climate [12–14]. DMSP is a starting material for both DMS and DMSO, and plants, algae and bacteria make it [15–18]. Because these DMSP-making organisms are so common in saltmarshes, they help drive the recycling of sulfur compounds made by living things (Fig. 1).

Earlier studies added DMSO to saltmarsh mud mixed with water and kept without oxygen. The DMSO was turned into DMS, and the DMS was then used up while methane was made at the same time [19, 20]. So the way DMSO is recycled in saltmarsh mud affects how much of three gases are made. Carbon dioxide (CO2) and methane (CH4) trap heat and warm the planet, while DMS reflects sunlight and cools it. Saltmarshes cover only about 0.01% of the world's surface [21]. Even so, they produce an unusually large share of the DMS in the world, about 0.28% [22], and about 13% of the methane that comes from the sea [23]. Saltmarshes also lock away carbon, which is why they are sometimes called blue carbon ecosystems. To model how they affect the climate, and how carbon and sulfur are recycled there, we need to understand what happens to DMS and DMSO in these places [24].

Fig. 1

A simple map of the sulfur compounds and enzymes that matter here.

DMS cools the climate and methane warms it. DMSO is broken down by DMSO-breaking enzymes (DmsA, DorA, TorA, TorZ). It can also be changed by DMS dehydrogenase (DdhA), trimethylamine (TMA)-monooxygenase (Tmm) or a monooxygenase made of several parts (DsoBDE). DMS can be changed into methanethiol (MeSH) by DMS monooxygenase (DmoA). Enzymes called DMS methyltransferases (MtsAB, MtsD, MtsF, MtsH) move a methyl group from DMS, with methanethiol (MeSH) as a short-lived in-between product. The resulting compound, methyl-coenzyme M, is then turned into methane by the enzyme methyl-coenzyme M reductase (McrA). DMSP is broken down by many different DMSP lyases (DddL, DddQ, DddW, DddY, DddK, DddP, DddD, DddX), and most of them can also break down DMSOP. Nobody has yet found the enzymes that turn DMSP into DMSOP or back again.

In the sea, DMSO comes from three sources: bacteria make it, sunlight changes DMS in seawater into DMSO, and DMSO falls from the air with rain and snow [13, 25]. Bacteria make DMSO with the help of an enzyme called DMS dehydrogenase, whose working part is DdhA. This has been shown in the bacterium Rhodovulum sulfidophilum [10, 26]. Another enzyme, trimethylamine monooxygenase (Tmm), was found to change DMS into DMSO in very common sea microbes, such as Pelagibacter ubique (SAR11) and Ruegeria pomeroyi [27, 28]. A bacterium called Acinetobacter sp. strain 20B uses a monooxygenase made of several parts (DsoBDE) to turn DMS into DMSO [29].

DMSO is also made when bacteria and algae break down a compound called dimethylsulfoxonium propionate (DMSOP) [30], and six DMSP lyases have been shown to break DMSOP apart [31]. DMSO has also been found to be made by certain Rhodobacterales [32], Flavobacteriales [33] and, more recently, diatoms, which are tiny algae with glassy shells [34]. In these organisms, however, the enzymes that do the job are still unknown.

In saltmarsh mud without oxygen, we know only that DMSO is turned into DMS, from measurements in mud mixed with water and kept in bottles [19, 20]. We still know little about which microbes do this, or how DMS is recycled without oxygen in these places. In fact, experiments without oxygen showed that different microbes in saltmarsh mud compete for DMSO and DMS [19, 35, 36]. As they used these compounds, they made methane or carbon dioxide, with DMS and methanethiol (MeSH) as short-lived in-between products.

What happens to DMS may depend on how much of it there is. When DMS levels are high, methane-making microbes that feed on small sulfur compounds take the lead. When DMS levels are low, microbes that breathe sulfate take the lead [19, 37]. DMSO is broken down by DMSO-breaking enzymes, of which two main types have been described in the bacterium Escherichia coli and in Rhodobacter species. These are called the Dms-type and the Dor-type [38, 39]. Both belong to a larger family of DMSO-breaking enzymes [10]. This family also includes closely related enzymes that break down a compound called trimethylamine-N-oxide. These enzymes often do two jobs at once, and some of them (TorZ) or possibly others (TorA) can also break down DMSO [9, 40].

We still do not know which enzymes bacteria use to break down DMS without oxygen. However, the enzymes that let methane-making microbes break down DMS have been described in Methanosarcina species. In Methanosarcina barkeri, for example, a team of enzymes made of the parts MtsAB moves the methyl groups from DMS onto a helper molecule called coenzyme M. This forms methyl-CoM, a key building block for making methane [41]. Methanosarcina acetivorans, on the other hand, can use the proteins MtsD or MtsF, which each have two working parts. These proteins move the methyl group in two steps to form methyl-CoM [42, 43]. Recently, groups of microbes that may make methane from DMS were described in sea mud and in mud that is covered and uncovered by the tides [36, 44]. But we still do not know which of them live in saltmarsh mud.

We set out to fill these gaps. We wanted to find and measure the compounds, the organisms and the key genes involved in turning DMSO into DMS and then breaking DMS down, in the typical zones of a saltmarsh. We had three ideas to test. First, we expected the amounts of sulfur compounds made by living things to differ between the zones. Second, we expected that the DMS made from DMSO could then be broken down further by particular methane-making microbes. Third, we expected that the genes for the enzymes in these steps would be especially common in the mixed DNA of the whole community, both from our bottle experiments and from natural saltmarsh samples.

To test these ideas, we measured DMSO and DMSP in two saltmarshes, one on Spiekeroog Island in Germany and one at Stiffkey in Norfolk, UK (Fig. S1, Tab. S1). We sampled them across clearly defined zones and at different depths in the mud. We kept samples from selected sites in sealed bottles without oxygen, so we could follow the order in which DMSO was turned into DMS and then DMS was broken down. To find out which microbes did this work, we used two approaches. First, we used statistics to look at how the variety of ribosomal RNA genes changed over time. These genes are found in every microbe, so they show which microbes are present. Second, we searched the mixed DNA of the whole community, from both our bottles and natural saltmarsh communities, for genes that carry the instructions for DMSO-breaking enzymes and for DMS methyltransferases.
parts.methods:
Materials and methods

Collecting the mud

We collected mud from two places. The first was the back barrier reef of the North Sea island Spiekeroog in Germany, where we sampled in July 2019, September 2019 and March 2020. The second was the Stiffkey saltmarsh in the United Kingdom, where we sampled in July 2021 (Fig. S1). We took every sample as a push core. This means we pushed a sterile syringe with its tip cut off into the mud and pulled out the mud inside, so we knew exactly how much we had (for example, 1 cm3). We then weighed each sample to find its density (Fig. S2, Tab. S1).

At Spiekeroog, we took mud from two depths, 0–1 cm and 4–5 cm, along three lines running from land to sea. These lines covered the upper saltmarsh (Upp), the lower saltmarsh (Low) and the pioneer zone (Pio), which is the first strip of land that forms as the marsh builds out toward the sea. We also sampled the shoreline (Edge) and the mudflat that is covered and uncovered by the tides (Mud). We took samples at every 1 cm step from the surface down to 6 cm. At Stiffkey, we sampled the same depths at three kinds of sites: places covered with the saltmarsh grass Spartina (Spar), bare areas with sandy mud (Sand), and muddy pools (Pool).

We also mixed together the top 5 cm of mud from Pio, Edge and Pool into one sample each. We used these for our bottle experiments and kept them at 4 °C until we needed them. We froze all samples for DNA work and for measuring DMSO right where we collected them. For measuring DMSP, we added 5 ml of 5 M sodium hydroxide (NaOH) to each sample and sealed it in the field. We carried the samples back and processed them for chemical measurements in sterile glass tubes, sealed with new butyl rubber stoppers pressed tightly in place.

Measuring gases in the air above the mud

We measured DMSP and DMSO twice for each sample. To do this, we first turned DMSP into DMS with a chemical [45] or DMSO into DMS with another chemical [46]. We then measured the DMS in the headspace, which is the pocket of air above the mud in a sealed container. For this we used headspace gas chromatography, a method that separates a gas mixture into its parts so that each one can be measured.

The samples had already started to break down DMSP chemically while we were preparing them in the field. To turn DMSO into DMS, we mixed 1 cm3 of mud into 5 ml of very pure water (ddH2O) and bubbled nitrogen through it for 18 minutes to strip out oxygen [47]. We then added 3.85 g of sodium metabisulfite (Na2S2O5), a chemical that turns DMSO into DMS. We heated the mixture at 60 °C for 10 minutes, then at 50 °C for 30 minutes, and finally at 1 °C for 5 minutes.

We measured DMS and methane (CH4) at a sample temperature of 30 °C. Samples from Spiekeroog went into an SRI 8610 C gas chromatograph (SRI Instruments, Bad Honnef, Germany). It had a stainless-steel column treated with Siltek (No. 70139–273; 30 m long and 0.28 mm wide, coated with MXT-1; Restek, Bad Homburg, Germany). The oven around the column was at 51 °C, argon gas carried the sample through the column, and a flame ionization detector (FID, 382 °C) detected the gases. We measured the size of each gas peak with the program Peak Simple V3.56 by SRI Instruments. Samples from Stiffkey went into a Shimadzu GC2010plus, as described in an earlier study [28].

We treated and measured standards of DMS, DMSO and DMSP in the same way as the samples. Standards are samples with a known amount of a substance, which let us turn our readings into concentrations. For methane standards, we used a gas mixture called N6 (No. 795.05106; Air Liquide, Düsseldorf, Germany). We calculated concentrations by assuming that all the methane had escaped into the headspace.

Bottle experiments

We combined the mud from three cores at each site (Pio, Edge and Pool) and mixed it well (Fig. S1, Tab. S1). We put about 2 cm3 of mud into each 100 ml serum bottle, together with 20 ml of a sterile, oxygen-free basic liquid food for microbes, called a basal medium. We based this medium on one from an earlier study [48]. Each liter of very pure water (ddH2O) contained 0.2 g KH2PO4, 0.25 g NH4C1, 20 g NaC1, 3 g MgC12 ∙ 6H2O, 0.15 g CaC12 ∙ 2H2O, 0.3 g KC1 and 1.5 g Na2SO4. It also contained 0.25 mg of resazurin, a dye that changes color when oxygen is present.

We sterilized the medium by heating it under pressure in an autoclave, which also removes the oxygen. After that, we added the following from sterile stock solutions: 1 ml of trace element solution SL10 [49], 1 ml of selenite-tungstate solution, 30 ml of 1 M NaHCO3, 1 ml of 0.2 M Na2S [48], and either 2 ml of 7-vitamin solution [50] or 10 ml of 10-vitamin solution [51]. We used the 7-vitamin solution for the Spiekeroog experiments and the 10-vitamin solution for the Stiffkey experiments. We did all transfers while flushing with nitrogen gas, so that the medium stayed free of oxygen after the autoclave had removed it.

We set up three bottles each of three treatments. The treatments were 1 mM DMSO (DMSO), 1 mM DMSO plus 10 mM sodium molybdate (DMSO + Mo), and no addition (Control). We used Spiekeroog mud from July 2019 (Pio and Edge) and Stiffkey mud from July 2021 (Pool). Molybdate (Na2MoO4) blocks the microbes that breathe sulfate. Adding it let us test how much these microbes might contribute to turning DMSO into DMS and to removing DMS.

We took samples for DNA work at the start (T0) and at the end (T2) of the experiments. We decided when an experiment had ended by whether DMS had run out and methane had leveled off. Each sample used up the bottle, so we set up one extra set of three bottles for the Stiffkey experiments to catch the point when DMS was highest (T1). We also ran extra experiments with Spiekeroog mud from September 2019. These compared how different amounts of DMSO, from 1 mM DMSO (DMSO) down to 0.1 mM DMSO (0.1 mM DMSO), affected how much DMS and methane were made. In all experiments, we followed DMS and methane production as described above.

Getting DNA out of the mud and reading it

For each saltmarsh site, we mixed three 1 cm3 samples together to make one combined sample. To collect the mud from the bottle experiments, we spun the bottles very fast in a centrifuge and poured off the liquid on top. We took 0.25–0.5 g of mud and pulled out its DNA with the DNeasy PowerSoil Pro Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany), following the maker's instructions. We checked the quality and amount of DNA with a NanoDrop 2000c (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Bremen, Germany) and stored the samples at −20 °C until we needed them.

To find out which microbes were present, we read a gene called the 16S rRNA gene. All bacteria and archaea carry this gene, but it differs between groups, so it works like a name tag. We read one stretch of it, the V4-V5 region, using two primers [52]. Primers are short pieces of DNA that mark where copying should start and stop. Ours were 515F-Y (5′-GTGYCAGCMGCCGCGGTAA-3′) and 926 R (5′-CCGYCAATTYMTTTRAGTTT-3′). We copied the gene and prepared it for reading as described in an earlier study [53], on a NovaSeq PE250 machine (Illumina, Berlin, Germany).

We also read all the DNA in some samples, a method called shotgun metagenome sequencing. This gave us a much fuller picture of the community. We used a NovaSeq 6000 system (Illumina) to read each DNA piece from both ends, 150 letters from each end (2 × 150 bp). We did this for samples from the Spiekeroog sites (July 2019) and from the Stiffkey bottle experiments.

Sorting the 16S rRNA gene data

We processed the 16S rRNA gene data with the program qiime2-2021.2 [54], which runs a cleaning method called DADA2 [55], as described in an earlier study [55]. This gave us counts of amplicon sequence variants (ASVs). Each ASV is one exact version of the gene, which roughly stands for one kind of microbe. We adapted our scripts from the collection at https://github.com/jcmcnch/eASV-pipeline-for-515Y-926R and ran them in a standard conda environment, a ready-made software setup.

We trimmed off the primer sequences and other unwanted parts with the program cutadapt [56], allowing a 20% mismatch in the primer sequence. Next, we sorted the 16S rRNA gene sequences using bbtools and the reference database SILVA138 [57]. We removed low-quality ends, where the median quality score was below 30, by trimming the forward and reverse sequences to a length of 220 bp. We then used qiime2 dada2 [58] to clean out reading errors, join the two ends of each piece, and remove chimeras. Chimeras are false sequences made when two different pieces of DNA get stuck together during copying. We named the microbes with the qiime2 classify-sklearn tool, using SILVA138 as the reference database. We left out sequences that came from chloroplasts or mitochondria, the parts inside plant and animal cells that carry their own 16S rRNA gene.

Putting the mixed DNA together and naming the genes

We pieced the mixed DNA together into longer stretches, called contigs, as described in an earlier study [59], with some changes. For the Stiffkey bottle experiments, we grouped gene sequences that were at least 95% identical using usearch 10.0.24 [60] (-cluster_fast –id 0.95). This gave us a gene catalog without repeats, as described before. It contained 8.51 × 10^6 representative gene sequences, and 1.62 × 10^9 reads matched to it (65% of all sequences).

The Spiekeroog mixed DNA was very varied and had been read in great depth, so grouping was not possible there. Instead, we removed duplicate sequences from the gene catalog with usearch 10.0.24 [60] (-fastx_uniques). This left 4.44 × 10^7 unique sequences, and 1.64 × 10^9 reads matched to them (75% of all sequences). We named the sequences by which organism they came from (Kaiju 1.6) [61] and by what they do (GhostKOALA) [62], as described before.

Some samples had been read more deeply than others, and genes differ in length. To make fair comparisons, we divided each read count by the gene length in thousands of letters (kb), giving reads per kilobase (rpk). We then divided the total for each sample by one million, giving reads per kilobase per million (rpkm).

We looked for genes for the enzymes that move the small carbon-and-sulfur piece (a methyl group) from DMS. These are the methylthiol:coenzyme M methyltransferase MtsAB and the methyl transferases MtsDFH, which are related to the genes MA0859, MA4384 and MA4558 of the microbe Methanosarcina acetivorans [42]. We found them with the program DIAMOND BLASTp [63], using the reference sequences Q48924, Q8PUA8 and Q48925 (UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot), as well as WP_048064984.1, WP_011024263.1 and WP_011024431.1 (NCBI). We counted a match only if more than 70% of its building blocks (amino acids) were identical and its e-value was below 1 × 10^−29. The e-value tells how likely a match this good would be to turn up by chance, so a very small value means a chance match is unlikely.

Sorting the mixed DNA into genomes and naming the genes

We sorted the contigs into groups, called bins, that each belong to one kind of microbe. This is called binning. First, we measured how many reads covered each contig using SAMtools v1.15.1–12g31dbb4 [64]. We then binned the contigs with metaBAT2 v2 [65]. We checked the quality of the bins with CheckM v1.2.0 [66] for the Spiekeroog mixed DNA and with CheckM2 v1.0.2 [67] for the Stiffkey mixed DNA. We kept only good-quality bins, which were more than 50% complete and had less than 5% contamination from other microbes. These became the genomes we pieced together from the mixed DNA.

Of all the reads, 5.80 × 10^8 (23%) matched the genomes from the Stiffkey samples, and 5.39 × 10^8 (25%) matched the genomes from the Spiekeroog samples. We placed the genomes on the family tree of life using the GTDB-Toolkit classify_wf [68]. We named the genes by what they do with GhostKOALA and DIAMOND BLASTp, as described above.

Much more of the mixed DNA matched the genomes (65% and 75%) than the genomes matched the mixed DNA (23% and 25%). So we did most of our analyses with the mixed DNA, which gives a sharper picture. We studied the individual genomes to learn about the possible chemical pathways the microbes could use.

Statistics and graphs

We did all statistics and graphs in R version 4.1.2 [69], using tidyverse v 2.0.0 [70] for most of the data handling. We found ASVs that were more or less common in one group than another with the program DESeq2 [71]. We compared samples grouped by treatment, time point and site.

For this, we kept only 16S rRNA gene sequences that had at least 20 reads in at least 3 samples. We added 1 read to every count, because DESeq2 cannot handle counts of zero. We then added shrunken log2 fold changes (LFC) and standard errors (SE) [72]. The log2 fold change shows how many times more common an ASV is in one group than in another, on a scale where 1 means twice as common. The standard error shows how uncertain that estimate is. We also applied a variance stabilizing transformation, which evens out how much the counts vary so that rare and common ASVs can be compared fairly.

We counted an ASV as significantly more common than in the controls if it had a Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p value of 0.05 or less and a log2 fold change of 0.5 or more. A p value of 0.05 means that, if there were really no difference, a gap this large would appear by chance alone less than 5% of the time. The Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment corrects for the fact that we tested many ASVs at once, which would otherwise make chance results look significant more often.
parts.results:
## Results

### DMSP and DMSO were most common near the shore and became scarcer deeper in the mud

We did not find DMS in any mud sample. DMSP and DMSO, however, turned up in most samples from both Spiekeroog (in Germany) and Stiffkey (in the UK) (Fig. 2, Table S2). We give amounts in nanomoles per gram of mud (nmol∙g−1). A nanomole is a very small, fixed number of molecules, so this unit tells us how many molecules of a compound are packed into each gram of mud.

On Spiekeroog, DMSP and DMSO became more common as we moved from the land towards the pioneer zone (Pio, sampled in March 2020) and then towards the shoreline (Edge, sampled in July 2019). The pioneer zone is the strip of marsh where plants first settle on bare ground. In July 2019, DMSP reached 154 ± 102 nmol∙g−1, more than in the samples taken in March 2020, which held 88 ± 63 nmol∙g−1. The number after the ± sign shows how much the measurements varied.

In every depth profile, both compounds dropped steeply within the top 2 cm of mud. DMSP fell from 155 ± 97 nmol∙g−1 in the top 0–1 cm to 23 ± 28 nmol∙g−1 in the 1–2 cm layer. DMSO fell from 36 ± 11 to 9 ± 6 nmol∙g−1 over the same layers.

In some samples we measured both compounds at the same time (September 2019, March 2020 and July 2021). There, DMSP was 3 to 4 times higher than DMSO: 43 ± 69 nmol∙g−1 of DMSP compared with 11 ± 17 nmol∙g−1 of DMSO. The mud pool at Stiffkey (Pool) was the exception. In its top 0–1 cm, DMSO was higher than DMSP, at 13.3 ± 2.3 compared with 4.2 ± 0.1 nmol∙g−1. Even so, the mud pool generally had the lowest average amounts of both compounds across all depth profiles: 1.4 ± 1.4 nmol∙g−1 of DMSP and 5.7 ± 4.2 nmol∙g−1 of DMSO.

The mud held a lot of DMSO, with an average of 11 nmol∙g−1 and a maximum of 106 nmol∙g−1. This shows that DMSO is available in these saltmarsh muds for microbes to use as a substance they can breathe without oxygen.

Fig. 2

DMSP and DMSO at the saltmarsh sampling sites.

A A line of sampling sites running from land to sea on Spiekeroog (DE). B DMSP and DMSO at different depths at selected sites on Spiekeroog (green) and in the Stiffkey saltmarsh (purple). We sampled in September 2019 (Spiekeroog) and July 2021 (Stiffkey).

### Reading the community's DNA showed which genes and microbes handle sulfur compounds

We read the DNA of the whole microbial community in the Spiekeroog samples, a method called metagenome analysis (Fig. 3). The genes for making DMSP (dsyB) and for turning DMS into DMSO (tmm) were most common in the lower saltmarsh (Low). These genes did not peak at the same places as the DMSP and DMSO themselves (Fig. 2), which hints that the compounds also come from other sources.

The genes that let microbes breathe DMSO (torA, torZ and dmsA) became steadily more common from land to sea. This mostly matched the pattern of DMSO amounts. The one exception was the mudflat samples (Mud), where the DMSO-breathing genes were common but DMSO was low.

The dmsA gene was common in three groups of bacteria: Zoogloeaceae, Enterobacterales and Desulfobacteraceae. In the mudflat samples, it reached up to 9.6 ± 1.0, 3.1 ± 0.3 and 1.6 ± 0.2 rpkm, respectively. Rpkm is a way of counting genes in DNA: it tells us how many copies of a gene there are, adjusted for how much DNA we read and how long the gene is. The Tor-type genes were generally less common than dmsA. Microbes carrying one of these DMSO-breathing genes included Rhodobacteraceae, Vibrionaceae, Pasteurellaceae, Desulfobulbaceae and Campylobacteraceae.

We also identified microbes by reading a gene called 16S rRNA, which works like a name tag for each kind of microbe (Fig. S3). Some of the groups above also showed up this way. For example, Rhodobacteraceae were present in every sample, and the microbes that breathe sulfate (such as Desulfobacteria and Desulfobulbia) made up a larger share of the community towards the sea. All the genes we studied for breaking down DMSO, and for making DMSP and DMSO, were found within the Rhodobacteraceae. This underlines their key role in recycling sulfur compounds in saltmarshes.

We also compared the DMSO-breathing enzymes we found with known ones. We did this both in the genomes we pieced together from the community's DNA and in the mixed DNA of the whole community, using only sequences longer than 600 amino acids (the building blocks of proteins). We built a family tree of these sequences. The vast majority grouped with the known DmsA, TorA and TorZ proteins (Fig. S6). Only some sequences fell into separate branches with no clear link to these DMSO-breathing proteins or to a closely related enzyme, biotin sulfoxide reductase (BisC).

We also checked whether the enzymes are sent out of the cell. A few sequences (bin 148-2, ID434, ID1597, ID235 and ID1351) were exceptions. All the TorZ and TorA sequences we used for the family tree had a signal for the TAT export pathway, a route that carries proteins out of the cell (checked with the program SignalP v5.0 [73]). The BisC enzymes of E. coli (P20099) and Cereibacter sphaeroides (P54934) did not have this signal.

Fig. 3

Gene counts and the microbes carrying them for DMSO-breathing genes along the land-to-sea line at Spiekeroog.

A Average (n = 3) total counts of each gene in each zone (Upp, Low, Pio, Mud). B Average (n = 3) total counts of each gene in each sample, with the microbes carrying them. "Others" are groups that made up less than 2% of the total counts of that gene.

### Adding DMSO to bottles of mud made the DMSO-breathing microbes from the saltmarsh more common

In every experiment where we added DMSO, DMS was being made from the very start (Fig. 4A). We saw no waiting period before DMS appeared (Fig. S4). This shows that a community of microbes able to break down DMSO was already living in the mud.

We also had control bottles, which got no added DMSO. They held 2 cm3 of mud from the top 0–5 cm, which had different amounts of DMSO in nature (see above). We did not detect any DMS coming from the mud itself. This suggests that DMS came only from DMSO being broken down.

We expected very little DMS in the controls. We used bulk mud (0–5 cm) with varying amounts of DMSO, and the bottles were 100 ml serum flasks with a lot of air space. The amount of DMS we expected was close to or below what we could detect (about 30 nmol in the bottles). In terms of molecules, breaking down all the DMSO in a 20 ml bottle would make at most 20 µmol of DMS. A µmol (micromole) is a millionth of a mole, so it is a thousand times more than a nanomole.

The highest DMS amounts ranged from 18.4 ± 1.8 to 20.3 ± 2.5 µmol in the DMSO treatments. In the DMSO + Mo treatments, where we added molybdate to block the microbes that breathe sulfate, they ranged from 13.2 ± 8.7 to 21.1 ± 0.5 µmol. That works out to 0.7–1.1 molecules of DMS for every molecule of DMSO we added (Table S3).

Fig. 4

DMSO experiments with saltmarsh mud from Spiekeroog (Pio and Edge, July 2019) and Stiffkey (Pool, July 2021).

A DMS (blue) and methane (CH4, black) made in the experiments. Colored bars mark when we took samples for DNA analysis: T0 at the start (blue), T1 after DMS peaked (red, only Stiffkey), and T2 at the end of the experiments, when methane had leveled off and all DMS was gone (green; 11 days for Spiekeroog, 13.5 days for Stiffkey). B Average share of each type of microbe (ASV) in all three experiments (Pio, Edge, Pool) that became statistically significantly more common because of the treatment (n = 3, deseq2, p ≤ 0.05, log2 fold change ≥ 0.5). ASVs shown made up more than 1% of the community in at least one sample; the rest are grouped as "Others".

To see which microbes changed, we sorted the 16S rRNA name-tag sequences into ASVs (amplicon sequence variants). Each ASV is one exact version of the name-tag, so it stands for one kind of microbe. Some shifts were easy to see at the level of large groups, such as Methanosarcinaceae. Smaller changes, such as in Rhodobacteraceae, were hard to show in an overview bar chart (Fig. S5).

So we used a method called differential community analysis (DESeq2) to compare the ASVs between treatments. It showed statistically significant increases (p ≤ 0.05, log2 fold change ≥ 0.5) of certain microbes in the DMSO and DMSO + Mo treatments compared with the control (Fig. 4B). A result is called statistically significant when, if there were really no difference, a gap this large would rarely appear by chance alone (here, 5% of the time or less). For example, Vibrionales made up a larger share of the community in DMSO and DMSO + Mo at the time DMS peaked (T1). Rhodobacterales increased only in DMSO + Mo at T1, while the microbes that breathe sulfate (Desulfobacterales and Desulfobulbales) became more common in the DMSO treatments.

Every one of these groups has been shown to break down DMSO, either in experiments (Table S4) or because members of the group carried one of the DMSO-breathing genes dmsA, torA or torZ in the community DNA (Fig. 5). Just as at the Spiekeroog sites, dmsA was the most common DMSO-breathing gene in the DNA from the Stiffkey bottles, at 105 ± 6 rpkm. Next came torZ (6 ± 3 rpkm) and torA (1 ± 1 rpkm).

The total number of dmsA genes was similar in the controls and the treatments, but the microbes carrying them differed. In the DMSO treatment, dmsA genes from groups such as Desulfobacteraceae, Enterobacteriaceae and Vibrionales became more common, but in the DMSO + Mo bottles they became less common. Zoogloeaceae (all Thauera sp. MZ1T) showed the opposite trend, with more dmsA in DMSO + Mo. Candidatus Aminicenantes was one of the few groups with more dmsA in both treatments.

The Tor-type genes (torA and torZ) were less common overall than dmsA, but they rose a lot because of the treatments. This happened for genes from Shewanellaceae, Enterobacteriaceae, Pasteurellaceae and Vibrionaceae in both treatments, and for Rhodobacteraceae in DMSO + Mo only.

Fig. 5

Gene counts and the microbes carrying them for DMSO-breathing genes in the Stiffkey saltmarsh bottles at the time DMS peaked (T1).

A Total counts of each gene in each sample. B Change in counts because of the treatment, with the microbes carrying them. Counts are the treatment (DMSO or DMSO + Mo) minus the control. Negative values (red) are lower in the treatment than in the control; positive values (blue) are higher. "Others" are groups that made up less than 2% of the total counts of that gene.

The bacteria that became more common in the bottle experiments also carried DMSO-breathing genes in the Spiekeroog samples. From the community DNA, we pieced together 80 genomes of individual microbes from the saltmarsh samples (Spiekeroog) and 331 from the bottle experiments (Stiffkey). In total, 14 of these genomes carried either one of the genes we studied for turning DMS into DMSO or one for making DMSP (Table S5). Only 3 genomes, all from the genus Vibrio, carried at least one of the DMSO-breathing genes for DmsBAD, TorAC or TorZY. These three also carried genes for TorS, TorT, TorD and TorR, but we could not find the gene for DmsC (K00185, K07308).

### Most of the DMS made from DMSO was used to make methane

In the bottle experiments, DMSO was turned into DMS, and then the DMS was used up while methane was made at the same time (Fig. 3A). The controls made almost no methane (0.3 ± 0.3 µmol or less). In some experiments, methane-making had started before DMS peaked. This probably lowered the peak DMS amounts and the number of DMS molecules made per DMSO molecule.

When microbes make methane from DMS, they use 1.5 molecules of DMS for each molecule of methane [74]. So the most methane we could expect from the 20 µmol of DMSO we added was 30 µmol. In our experiments, peak methane amounts were between 21.0 ± 1.8 and 26.1 ± 2.4 µmol. That is 1.1–1.3 molecules of methane for every molecule of DMSO. So most of the DMS made from DMSO was used to make methane.

The DMSO + Mo and DMSO treatments differed slightly. At Edge, they made 24.3 ± 1.4 and 22.2 ± 0.8 µmol of methane, and at Pio, 26.1 ± 2.4 and 23.6 ± 3.2 µmol. This may be because blocking the microbes that breathe sulfate stopped them from using up DMS, leaving more for the methane-making microbes. In the Pool bottles, however, the trend was reversed: DMSO + Mo made 21.0 ± 1.8 µmol and DMSO made 23.8 ± 0.8 µmol.

We expected that turning DMS into methane would leave behind simple sulfur compounds, such as hydrogen sulfide (H2S). Over time, the share of Thiotrichales and Thiomicrospirales, two groups of microbes that breathe sulfur compounds, went up in both treatments. At T2, Thiomicrorhabdus reached up to 2% ± 1 of the community in the DMSO + Mo treatments.

In extra experiments (September 2019), DMS peaked after 2 days in bottles with 0.1 mM DMSO (Fig. S3). This was earlier than in bottles with more DMSO, where it took 6 days. The number of DMS molecules made per DMSO molecule was 0.3 at Edge and 0.5 at Pio. That is lower than in the matching 1 mM DMSO treatments, where it was 0.4 at Edge and 1.1 at Pio (Table S3). This suggests that the amount of DMSO, and so the amount of DMS made, affected the competition for DMS between the methane-making microbes and other microbes that break it down.

### MtsD and MtsH were the main enzymes that move methyl groups in making methane from DMS

As DMS was used up to make methane, the share of Methanosarcinales in the 16S rRNA data rose significantly (Fig. 4). They made up as much as 17% ± 14 of all bacteria and archaea at T2. This was mainly due to Methanolobus species in the Stiffkey samples, which made up 40% ± 1.7 of the community. Other archaea rose only slightly at T2 (Methanococcoides and ANME-3). Earlier work reported that members of Methanolobus and Methanococcoides are methane-making microbes that feed on small sulfur compounds [75]. They became more common while DMS was being used up and methane was being made, which suggests they were the main DMS users in the bottles.

We searched all the community DNA for three genes (Fig. 6). The first was mcrA, the marker gene for making methane. The other two, mtsA and mtsB, carry the instructions for the methyltransferase and the corrinoid parts of the methylthiol:coenzyme M methyltransferase. A methyltransferase is an enzyme that moves a methyl group from one molecule to another.

The mcrA genes became more common in the bottles (T2), but in the Spiekeroog samples they were very rare (less than 0.2 rpkm). We did not find mtsA or mtsB in any sample. So we ran a second search with the program DIAMOND BLASTp, which looks for similar protein sequences. This search included mtsAB and the joined-up corrinoid/methyltransferase protein MtsDFH, which is involved in growing on DMS in the microbe Methanosarcina acetivorans. We still did not find MtsAB. But we did find MtsDFH-like sequences from the Methanosarcinaceae in the DNA from the DMSO and DMSO + Mo bottles. The program GhostKOALA had not matched any of these sequences to a known gene before.

Fig. 6

Gene counts and the microbes carrying them for mcrA (K00399, K00400) and mtsDFH in the Stiffkey saltmarsh bottles.

A Total counts of each gene in each sample. B Change in counts because of the treatment, with the microbes carrying them. Counts are the treatment minus the control (for example, T1-DMSO minus T1-Cont). Negative values (red) are lower in the treatment than in the control; positive values (blue) are higher.

We also pieced together three genomes of Methanolobus (bin95, bin151 and bin173) from the bottle DNA. We searched them for genes for enzymes thought to take part in making methane from DMS [76]. This let us rebuild most of the full chain of steps in all three genomes (Fig. 7, Table S6).

In short, MtsD moves both methyl groups of DMS onto coenzyme M (CoM), a small helper molecule. It does this in two steps, first forming methanethiol (MeSH) and then two CoM-CH3 molecules. Each methyl group can then go one of two ways. It can be passed to tetrahydromethanopterin (H4MPT) by MtrA-H, and then CO2 is released. Or it can be turned into methane while coenzyme B (CoB) joins with CoM to form CoB-S-S-CoM.

Several helper molecules would then need to be reset. CoM, CoB and coenzyme F420 would likely be reset by the F420H2 dehydrogenase (FpoA-O), the membrane-bound heterodisulfide reductase (HdrDE) and the Na+-translocating ferredoxin complex (RnfA-G), respectively. Ferredoxin (Fdred) is a small iron-and-sulfur protein that carries electrons. Fpo and HdrD could possibly also reset CoM, CoB and F420 together [76]. However, we did not find any of the other enzymes that could take electrons from ferredoxin in any of the genomes. These include the coenzyme F420-reducing hydrogenase (FrhABG), the energy-conserving hydrogenase (EhbA-Q) and the [NiFe]-hydrogenase (VhtGACD).

All three genomes carried genes for the soluble heterodisulfide reductase HdrABC. However, we found none of the genes for the enzymes that supply the electrons this enzyme needs (for example, the formate dehydrogenase FdhAB or the F420-non-reducing hydrogenase MhvAGD). As the suggested steps run, hydrogen ions (H+) and sodium ions (Na+) are pushed across the cell's membrane. This builds up a difference in H+ and Na+ across the membrane, a bit like water held behind a dam. The ATPase (AtpVA-VK) can use this difference to make ATP, the cell's energy currency.

To check that our BLASTp matches were correct, we built a family tree of the MtsDFH sequences we found (longer than 400 amino acids), using closely related known sequences as its backbone (Fig. S7). In the bottle DNA, most of the sequences were MtsD (36.5 rpkm in DMSO and 48.0 rpkm in DMSO + Mo). MtsH came next (5.2 rpkm in DMSO and 3.9 rpkm in DMSO + Mo), while MtsF was almost absent (less than 0.02 rpkm).

We found mcrA and mtsDH in both Methanococcoides and Methanolobus, which shows that these microbes can make methane from DMS. In contrast, we did not find the mcrA gene in the group with the most mtsD, Methanohalophilus.

Discussion

Sulfur compounds made by living things matter for how carbon and sulfur move through the environment. For decades, scientists have studied the separate steps, the microbes and the genes involved in turning DMSO into DMS when oxygen is present [77–79]. Most studies that read DNA directly from the environment, without first growing microbes in the lab, have focused on how DMS and DMSP are made and broken down in the sea [15, 80–84]. Only a few have also looked at microbes turning DMSO into DMS [85, 86].

Scientists have long known that microbes breathing DMSO in place of oxygen release DMS. That DMS can then escape into the air, or microbes can break it down into methane (CH4) or carbon dioxide (CO2) [20]. DMS cools the climate, while methane warms it, so we need a full picture of what happens to both gases in nature.

DMSO has been measured in many kinds of seawater and fresh water, with the highest values at 620 nmol∙L−1 [87–89]. (A nanomole per litre, nmol∙L−1, is a way of counting how many molecules are dissolved in a litre of water.) So far, nobody has measured DMSO in mud from the sea. In our saltmarsh mud, the highest value we measured was 106.2 nmol∙g−1, meaning 106.2 nanomoles in each gram of mud. We worked out the amount per litre by multiplying this by the weight of the mud, 1.83 g∙cm−3 (Tab. S2). This gave 194.4 µmol∙L−1, which is about 300 times higher than the highest value in seawater. So the DMSO we added to our bottles (0.1 and 1 mM) may not have been unrealistically high.

In our bottles, DMSO was quickly turned into DMS (Fig. S4). In the natural mud, DMSO was used up within the top few centimetres. Both results show that saltmarshes hold a community of microbes that can turn DMSO into DMS. In the mud of the sea, where there is no oxygen, it has remained largely unknown what happens to DMSO and which microbes control how quickly it is used up.

Here, we built on the important early work of Kiene and Capone [20]. We used bottles of mud kept without oxygen, with DMSO added, and we added two DNA methods. The first, 16S rRNA gene sequencing, reads one gene that all bacteria and archaea carry, which tells us which microbes are present. The second, shotgun metagenomics, reads all the DNA in a sample at once. We combined these bottle experiments with the study of natural saltmarsh mud to find out which microbes drive the turning of DMSO into DMS, and which make methane from DMS.

In our bottles, the compounds we measured changed in a sequence over time. This matched patterns found in earlier studies [20, 36]. We can split the process into two clear phases, based on the amounts of DMS and methane in the air above the mud. In the first phase (from the start, T0, to T1), DMSO was turned into DMS. In the second (from T1 to T2), DMS was broken down and methane was made. We added DMSO to boost the microbes that carry out these steps. Even so, the two phases overlapped in our bottles. In nature, they most likely happen at the same time, or possibly in neighbouring layers of the mud.

DMSP, the starting material for the sulfur cycle

DMSP is thought to be the main source of DMS in the sea [90]. Our results show that DMSP and DMSO are easy to find in saltmarsh mud, where a varied community of bacteria that feed on ready-made food uses them up. The natural amounts of DMSP we found on Spiekeroog and in the Stiffkey saltmarsh (less than 300 nmol∙g−1) were within the range reported before [15, 80].

Along the line of sampling spots we set up across Spiekeroog, DMSP was highest at the shoreline (the spot we called Edge). In the lower saltmarsh (Low), we found many copies of the dsyB gene, which is needed to make DMSP. This hints that bacteria there may make more DMSP. In contrast, the pioneer zone (the first zone to form as the marsh develops) and the saltmarsh edge could be strongly shaped by other very common DMSP makers. These include the grass Spartina (also called Sporolobus) and diatoms, which are tiny algae with glassy shells [6, 16, 18].

The natural community that turns DMSO into DMS reacts readily when DMSO is added in bottle experiments

Many bacteria and archaea can turn DMSO into DMS (for example, the groups Actinobacteriota, Proteobacteria and Halobacterota; see Tab. S4). This is likely because the family of enzymes that does this job is very old [91]. Our DNA results from the bottles and the natural samples showed the same thing: the ability to turn DMSO into DMS is found almost everywhere [92]. We also found the microbes and genes linked to this process in the mixed DNA of the whole community, before sorting it into individual genomes. These were mostly the same in the natural saltmarshes and in the bottles, even though the two came from very distant places (Stiffkey in the UK and Spiekeroog in Germany).

Our bottle experiments suggest that molybdate, the chemical we used to block microbes that breathe sulfate, lowered the share of these microbes and of most other bacteria carrying the dmsA gene. Only a few groups of dmsA-carrying bacteria, such as Zoogloeaceae and Sporomusaceae, became more common when we added both DMSO and molybdate, but less common with DMSO alone. In the Spiekeroog DNA, Zoogloeaceae carried more dmsA genes than any other group, but no one has yet tested whether they can turn DMSO into DMS in the lab.

Looking more closely, we matched members of Zoogloeaceae and Sporomusaceae to Thauera sp. MZ1T and Acetonema longum. Neither is known for breathing sulfate [93, 94]. Taken together, microbes that breathe sulfate may not be able to make up fully for the loss of sulfate breathing by turning DMSO into DMS. They could also compete less well for DMSO where there is little sulfate. This supports the findings of Jonkers and colleagues [95]: for example, the bacterium Desulfovibrio desulfuricans could not grow by turning DMSO into DMS when its sulfate breathing was blocked.

In contrast, bacteria carrying the Tor-type of DMSO-breaking enzyme appeared in the bottles with DMSO and molybdate. This points to Rhodobacterales or Vibrionales competing better when sulfate is low. In our bottles, we pieced together three genomes from Vibrio. In each, we found most of the extra genes of the DMSO-breaking enzyme gene sets, as well as the marker genes we had chosen to track (dmsA, torA and torZ) [10]. This supports the idea that these microbes can turn DMSO into DMS, possibly even with more than one way of doing it.

In earlier experiments, adding DMSO switched on the TorA gene. In our treatments (DMSO alone, and DMSO with molybdate), the number of TorA genes also went up. However, TorA has been shown to grab DMSO only weakly [96]. So the rise we saw may also come from Vibrionaceae and Shewanellaceae growing by using one of the other DMSO-breaking enzymes (TorZ or DmsA).

Today, the KEGG database, a large catalogue of genes and what they do, has no entry of its own for DorA. So we tried to find DorA genes using the search patterns (called hmm profiles) provided with the DiTing-pipeline software [86]. This approach relabelled some sequences as DorA that had been labelled as TorA, TorZ or BisC (an enzyme called biotin sulfoxide reductase) by the program GhostKOALA and by family trees of the genes (data not shown). The only DorA sequence in the UniProt database that has been checked by experts (Q52675) is labelled as TorZ by GhostKOALA. So our approach likely counted possible DorA sequences as TorZ.

TorZ, DorA and BisC are very similar, which makes it hard for any method that labels genes by how similar they look. Still, one feature supports the GhostKOALA labels. TorZ and TorA carry a short tag called the twin arginine motif, which the TAT pathway needs to carry proteins across the cell's outer membrane. BisC lacks this tag.

Making methane from DMS, and other things DMS can become

To make methane from DMS, a methyl group must first be moved from DMS onto a helper molecule called coenzyme M [41]. The two known kinds of enzymes that do this, MtsA and MtsDFH, have been found in lab cultures of methane-making microbes [41, 42], but there are only a few reports of them in nature [97]. We did not find them in the saltmarshes we studied. This is probably because methane-making microbes are rare in the top layer of mud, and because of the amount of DNA we read. The mtsDFH gene is also poorly represented in the reference databases, and our strict search settings (using a program called DIAMOND BLASTp) may have missed it.

There might be other, still unknown, enzymes of this kind. Even so, MtsDH seem to be the main known ones. In our bottles, MtsAF was missing, the Methanosarcinaceae that carry MtsDH became more common, and three genomes we pieced together from the group Methanolobus carried MtsD.

Methane-making microbes that feed on small sulfur compounds have been seen in lab cultures of Methanohalophilus [98]. However, the two members that break down DMS, M. zhilinae and M. oregonense, have since been renamed Methanosalsum zhilinae and Methanolobus oregonensis [75, 99, 100]. The mcrA gene, which is needed to make methane, is present in all ten publicly available genomes of Methanohalophilus (as of 18.04.2023) in the IMG database (genome IDs: 2703719298, 2703719067, 2754412526, 2914862632, 2642422606, 2913510308, 646564550, 2806310721, 2914860506, 2706794887). But we could not find any genomes we pieced together that belonged to this group. Based on our findings and on the mcrA genes in these public genomes, we assume these archaea also make methane from DMS, but their mcrA gene did not show up in our DNA analysis.

In most of our experiments, the amount of methane made from DMS was close to the highest possible value, 1.5 molecules of methane per molecule of DMS [74, 101]. At the same time, the methane-making microbes that feed on small sulfur compounds (Methanosarcinales) became much more common. This supports the findings of Tsola and colleagues [36], who showed that making methane can use up a large amount of DMS in the mud of the shore, where there is no oxygen.

The amount of methane made from DMS was slightly lower than the highest possible value, especially when we added only 0.1 mM DMSO. This points to some of the DMS or DMSO being used up in another way. It supports the idea that microbes that break down DMS but do not make methane, such as microbes that breathe sulfate, compete better when DMS is scarce [19, 37, 102]. In some bottles, we saw more methane when we blocked sulfate breathing. This gives more evidence that microbes that breathe sulfate break down DMS, although it does not fully settle the question.

In our bottles without oxygen, the share of Thiotrichales went up. This does not clash with how these bacteria usually live. Most Thiotrichales are sulfur-oxidizing bacteria that need oxygen [103], and some can live without oxygen by breathing nitrate [104]. One member, Methylophaga thiooxydans, can grow on DMS with oxygen and turn sulfide into tetrathionate [105, 106]. Thiotrichales have also been seen near Methanosarcinales at places where methane leaks out of the ground [103]. Future work must find out whether, and how, these microbes help break down DMS or sulfide where there is no oxygen.
